title: Fourth down: go for it, punt or kick (and how to call it in your drill)
html:
Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this morning: it still holds one logged game file (data/games/gmum7mktl1wy3.json, last updated Oct 12) and no review files, and the original football-film-room repository wasn't reachable from this run (access denied: not configured for this session, and no tool to add it was available). So there's no new miss of yours to fix, and no snap of yours this connects to yet. This lesson picks up Monday night: Dallas pulled away from a 28-21 game after Philadelphia went for it on 4th down deep in its own territory and failed. It also matters for Thursday's pick: Green Bay is 30th in red-zone TD rate, and whether it kicks or goes for it on 4th-and-goal decides how many points go on the board.

The big idea: on 4th down the offense has one play left before the ball changes hands, and three choices: punt (give the ball back but push the other team about 40 yards away), kick a field goal (3 points, if it's close enough), or go for it (keep the drive if you make the yards; if you don't, the other team gets the ball right where you stopped). Two things decide most of it: where you are on the field and how many yards you need. The score and the clock bend both.

Top: the three zones (1–3), for an offense driving left to right; the yellow dot is roughly where Philadelphia went for it Monday. Bottom (4): how often teams make it, by yards needed (rounded, approximate). Numbers match the steps below.

  1. Your own end: punt (1). From your own 20, a punt moves the other team back about 40 yards. A failed try gives them the ball already in field-goal range, so it's usually worth 3 points or more to them. That's what Philadelphia risked Monday: behind in the 4th quarter with a backup quarterback, it gambled deep in its own territory, didn't make it, and Dallas (Brandon Aubrey 3 of 3 on field goals) pulled away. Trailing late changes the math (step 5); it doesn't remove the downside.
  2. No-man's land: go on short yardage (2). Between your own 40 and the opponent's 35, a field goal would be 52 yards or longer (Lesson 36: add 17 to the yard line), and a punt only gains 30 to 35 yards before it rolls into the end zone. That's why modern coaches go for it here on 4th-and-1 or 2. Detroit under Dan Campbell is the best-known example of a team that does this almost every time.
  3. Field-goal range: kick, unless it's 4th-and-1 (3). Inside the opponent's 35, 3 points are close to certain from an NFL kicker. The exception is very short yardage, especially near the goal line: on 4th-and-goal from the 1 or 2, a touchdown is worth 4 more points than the field goal, so many coaches go.
  4. Distance decides the rest (4). Roughly two in three 4th-and-1 tries succeed; by 4th-and-7 or longer, it's closer to one in four. Philadelphia built its 4th-and-1 game around the quarterback sneak with Jalen Hurts (Lesson 33); with Hurts out for the season, that near-automatic play is gone, which is one more reason its 4th downs are riskier now.
  5. The score and clock bend the zones (Lesson 23). A team trailing in the 4th quarter has fewer possessions left, so a punt "costs" more and going for it moves into the punt zone; a team protecting a lead does the opposite and kicks. In college, the same logic holds, but more kickers are shaky from 45+ yards, so the no-man's land is wider.
  6. For your bets. In the red zone, the 4th-down choice is a 4-point swing (touchdown 7 vs. field goal 3), which is often the difference on a total. Green Bay (30th in red-zone TD rate) settling for field goals is part of the Under 47.5 case Thursday; a Green Bay coach going for it on 4th-and-goal works against it. On the spread, a failed try in your own end usually hands the other team 3 points or more.

How to log it in your drill: on 4th-and-1 or less with the quarterback under center and extra tight ends or linemen in (12 or 13 personnel, Lesson 1), call RUN: a sneak or an inside run is the usual play. On 4th-and-3 or longer, or anytime it's shotgun with 3+ receivers, call PASS. If the punt or field-goal unit comes out, note it as special teams; if they then run a fake, that's a gadget play (Lesson 35), and the drill scores it by what actually happened.

Real examples to watch: Thursday, Panthers at Packers (Fri 9:15 a.m. JST / Thu 5:15 p.m. PT, Prime Video): Green Bay's choices inside the 10. Saturday in college, Ohio State at USC (Sun 8:30 a.m. JST / Sat 4:30 p.m. PT, NBC). Sunday night, Eagles at Commanders (Mon 10:20 a.m. JST / Sun 5:20 p.m. PT, NBC): whether Nick Sirianni still goes for it with McKee at quarterback.

Video: search YouTube for "fourth down decision explained NFL," "Lions fourth down Dan Campbell," and "Eagles tush push explained."

Practice it in Football Camp → (Station 6: Situations)

quiz.q: It's 4th-and-2 at your own 25 in the 2nd quarter, tied. What do most coaches do?
o: Take a timeout and go for it
quiz.w: In your own end a failed try hands the other team a short field (often 3+ points). Punting moves them back about 40 yards.

quiz.q: Why is the area between your own 40 and the opponent's 35 called "no-man's land"?
o: It's too far for a reliable field goal and too close for a good punt
quiz.w: A kick from the opponent's 36 is about a 53-yarder, and a punt from midfield nets only 30 to 35 yards before the end zone. So short-yardage tries make the most sense there.

quiz.q: Roughly how often is 4th-and-1 converted in the NFL?
quiz.w: Approximately two out of three. By 4th-and-7 or longer it drops to about one in four.

quiz.q: In your drill: 4th-and-1, quarterback under center, two tight ends and a fullback in. What's the call?
quiz.w: Short yardage plus heavy personnel and the QB under center points to a sneak or inside run.
